rubric: Explains that aperture controls how much light enters and affects depth of field (wider aperture = shallower focus)
Explains that shutter speed controls exposure time and motion blur
Explains that raising ISO brightens the image but adds noise
Describes the trade-off: changing one setting to fix brightness changes the look, so the other two must compensate

resources.title: The exposure triangle explained

keyPoints: Exposure depends on aperture, shutter speed and ISO together

Slower shutter speeds add light and motion blur

resources.title: Exposure Triangle Basics: Aperture, Shutter Speed and ISO

keyPoints: Set shutter speed to about double the frame rate

explainBack.question: How would you light a talking-head video with three-point lighting, and how do you control how soft the light is and its color?
rubric: The key light is the main, brightest source, usually placed at an angle (around 45 degrees) in front of the subject
The fill light sits on the opposite side and is dimmer than the key (e.g. about a 2:1 key-to-fill ratio), lifting the shadows the key creates
The back (rim) light sits behind the subject and separates them from the background, adding depth
A source that is larger relative to the subject (diffused, bounced, softbox) gives softer, more gradual shadows; a small direct source gives hard, sharp shadows
Color temperature is measured in Kelvin (daylight about 5600K, tungsten about 3200K); avoid mixing sources of different color temperature and set white balance to match the light

resources.title: YouTube Lighting Setup for Beginners: 3 Point Lighting Tutorial

explainBack.question: How do you record clean dialogue for a video, and how do you set your levels?
rubric: Peaks should sit well below 0 dBFS to leave headroom; a common target is roughly -12 to -6 dBFS (some guides suggest a more cautious ceiling around -16 dB)
Digital clipping happens when the signal tries to exceed 0 dBFS; the waveform is cut off and the distortion cannot be fully fixed in post
Moving the mic closer to the mouth raises the voice relative to background noise and room reflections, rather than just turning up gain
Pick the mic and pickup pattern for the job: a lavalier for close, consistent dialogue; a shotgun just out of frame aimed at the mouth; cardioid/directional patterns reject off-axis sound
Monitor with isolating headphones while recording to hear noise, distortion or problems before it is too late

Focused on dialogue capture for video

resources.title: Techniques for Gaining Stage Your Microphone During Recording

keyPoints: Recommends peaks between -12 dB and -6 dB while recording

Move the mic closer instead of only adding preamp gain
Monitor on headphones; distortion at recording cannot be fully fixed in post

Omni handhelds can sit between two speakers; cardioid handhelds must be close

explainBack.question: What are the main shot sizes, and how do headroom, lead room and the 180-degree rule keep a video readable?
rubric: Names shot sizes and their uses: wide shots show the subject in their setting, medium shots (about waist up) balance subject and surroundings, close-ups show faces and emotion
Headroom is the space above the subject's head; too much makes them look like they are sinking, too little feels cramped or crops the head
Look/lead room is extra space in the direction the subject faces or moves, so the frame feels balanced and the viewer sees where they are going
180-degree rule: draw an imaginary line (axis of action) between subjects and keep the camera on one side so their left/right relationship and screen direction stay consistent
Rule of thirds: place key features such as the eyes on or near the thirds lines and intersections rather than dead center

stages.title: Editing Fundamentals
stages.description: Use J-cuts, L-cuts, jump cuts and cutting on action, and control pacing, to make edits feel smooth and keep viewers watching.

explainBack.question: Explain J-cuts, L-cuts, jump cuts and cutting on action, and when you'd use each.
rubric: J-cut: the audio of the next clip starts before its picture, useful to lead into a new scene or build anticipation
L-cut: the audio of the current clip continues over the next clip's picture, e.g. showing a listener's reaction in dialogue or interviews
Jump cut: a cut within the same shot that skips ahead in time; common in talking-head videos to remove pauses and filler words
Cutting on action: cutting during a movement so the motion carries the viewer's eye across the cut and hides it
Pacing: shot length and rhythm set the energy; faster cutting builds intensity, slower cutting gives room to breathe, and trimming dead air helps hold attention

stages.title: Color Correction & Grading

explainBack.question: What's the difference between color correction and color grading, and how do scopes help you do them?
rubric: Color correction comes first: fix exposure/contrast and white balance and make shots match so footage looks natural and consistent
Color grading comes after correction and applies a creative look or mood to the corrected footage
A waveform monitor shows the luminance (brightness) of the image, with brighter parts higher and darker parts lower on the graph
A vectorscope shows hue (angle around the circle) and saturation (distance from the center); skin tones of all people should fall near its skin-tone line
Log footage is intentionally flat/low-contrast to preserve dynamic range and must be converted (e.g., an input LUT or color space transform/color management) before grading

resources.title: Color Correction vs Color Grading Explained | Cinecom.net

resources.title: Color Grading vs. Color Correction Process for Video
resources.description: Defines correction as the technical step that makes footage look natural and consistent, and grading as the creative step that adds mood, and lays out the order to do them in.
keyPoints: Correction fixes color problems so footage looks natural and consistent
Grading adds atmosphere and emotion, often with stylized color
Workflow: set picture profile, then correct, then grade

stages.description: Make dialogue clear and levels consistent with loudness metering, EQ, compression and ducking so audio holds up after platform normalization.

explainBack.question: How do you make your video's audio sound clear and consistent across platforms?
rubric: Loudness is measured in LUFS (per ITU-R BS.1770); integrated loudness is the average over the whole program

Platforms normalize playback loudness: many streaming services target about -14 LUFS; YouTube publishes no official figure but is commonly measured around -12 to -14 LUFS and adjusts playback level to match
EQ shapes frequencies, e.g., a high-pass filter removes low-frequency rumble that muddies dialogue
Compression reduces dynamic range so quiet and loud parts end up closer in level
Ducking automatically lowers music while dialogue is present

explainBack.question: How does YouTube decide what to recommend, and which analytics tell you whether a video is working?
rubric: Recommendations are driven by viewer behavior and satisfaction signals (clicks, watch time, likes, dislikes, shares, survey responses); it is a constantly evolving learning system, not a fixed formula
An impression is counted when a video's thumbnail is shown on YouTube (at least 50% visible for over 1 second)
Impressions CTR is how often viewers watched after seeing an impression (views from impressions divided by impressions)
Audience retention and average view duration show how long people watch and where they drop off (intro, dips, spikes)
Use them together: low CTR points to title/thumbnail; poor retention points to content/pacing; high CTR with low view duration suggests misleading packaging

stages.title: Copyright, Licensing & Platform Policies
stages.description: Know the legal options for using others' music and clips, and what Content ID claims and copyright strikes mean for your channel.
learningObjectives: Distinguish public domain material from royalty-free/licensed material
Explain the conditions attached to Creative Commons licenses
Differentiate a Content ID claim from a copyright strike and their consequences
Explain why fair use is decided case by case and why giving credit is not enough
Identify safe music sources such as the YouTube Audio Library

explainBack.question: Can you use someone else's music or clip in your video? Explain the options and what happens if you get it wrong.
rubric: Public domain works (e.g., CC0-dedicated) have no copyright restrictions; 'royalty-free' is not the same - it is still a license, and you must follow its terms (e.g., attribution)
Creative Commons licenses allow use under conditions: Attribution (BY), NonCommercial (NC), NoDerivatives (ND), ShareAlike (SA)

A Content ID claim lets the rights holder block, monetize or track the video and does not by itself cause a strike; a copyright strike follows a valid legal removal request and removes the video, and three active strikes can get the channel terminated
Fair use is decided case by case by courts using four factors (purpose, nature, amount, market effect); crediting the creator or adding a disclaimer does not make a use fair
The YouTube Audio Library provides copyright-safe music that won't be claimed, though some tracks require attribution

resources.title: What can you do about Content ID claims? - Copyright on YouTube
resources.description: YouTube's official explainer on what a Content ID claim means for your video and the options you have in response.
keyPoints: What happens when Content ID matches your upload
Options such as removing the claimed content or disputing
Part of YouTube's official copyright series

resources.title: About CC Licenses
resources.description: Creative Commons' official description of the four license elements, the six licenses built from them, and the CC0 public domain dedication.
keyPoints: BY: credit the creator
SA: adaptations must use the same terms
NC: noncommercial use only; ND: no adaptations
Six licenses range from CC BY to CC BY-NC-ND
CC0 places a work in the public domain

resources.title: Use music and sound effects from the Audio Library
resources.description: Explains YouTube's free Audio Library, which tracks can be monetized, and when attribution is required.
keyPoints: Royalty-free, copyright-safe music and sound effects
Audio Library tracks won't be claimed via Content ID
Creative Commons tracks require crediting the artist
Standard-license tracks need no attribution
YouTube only vouches for its own library, not other royalty-free sources

resources.title: What is a copyright claim?
resources.description: Explains what a Content ID copyright claim is and what rights holders can do with it, and how it differs from a strike.
keyPoints: Content ID applies a claim when it finds matching content
Claimants can block, monetize or track the video
Actions can differ by country
Claims are separate from copyright strikes

resources.title: Copyright strike basics
resources.description: Explains when a copyright strike is issued, what happens with each strike, and the ways to resolve one.
keyPoints: A strike follows a valid legal copyright removal request
Strikes expire after 90 days if you complete Copyright School
Three strikes: account and channels subject to termination
Resolve via waiting, retraction or counter notification

resources.title: Fair use on YouTube
resources.description: YouTube's explanation of U.S. fair use: the four factors courts weigh, that outcomes depend on the facts, and common myths.
keyPoints: Four factors: purpose, nature, amount used, market effect
Courts decide each case on its own facts
Giving credit doesn't make a copy fair use
'No infringement intended' disclaimers don't protect you
